list.listitem: Gynecomastia can be physiologic or pathological. Pathological gynecomastia has to be differentiated from physiological gynecomastia, which is very common among adolesent boys during puberty with the majority resolving within 1-3 years. background.definition: Gynecomastia is a benign enlargement of the male breast caused by a proliferation of ductal elements and not simply excessive breast fatty tissue.

list.listitem: Most boys develop breast enlargement during puberty.
Most common in boys after 13 years and men >65 years.
Approximately one-third of normal men have palpable breast tissue.
Approximately two-thirds of hospitalized men have gynecomastia.
Gynecomastia occurs in 7% to 85% of men treated for prostate cancer (depending upon the specific therapy).
Normal puberty or aging.
Primary or secondary hypogonadism, including Klinefelter syndrome.
Medical conditions leading to altered estrogen-to-androgen ratio (such as HIV, liver disease, renal failure, etc).
Increased secretion of estrogen by testicular and adrenal tumors (Leydig cell tumors, Sertoli cell tumors, hCG-secreting tumors, etc).
Anti-androgen treatment of prostate cancer.

About 20% of the pathological gynecomastia are produced by medications or exogenous agents. Some of the chemotheraputic agents causing gynecomatia include methotrexate, alkylating agents, imatinib, vinca alkaloids.
Unintentional exposure to estrogen (vaginal estrogen cream absorption during intercourse, food from estrogen-treated plants and animals).

Other drugs including spironolactone, ketoconazole, calcium channel blockers, isoniazid, metronidazole, metoclopramide, and phenothiazines, thiazide diuretics, digoxin, some antiretroviral agens, PPIs, and HAART
Drugs of abuse including alcohol, marijuana, and amphetamines.
Imbalance between stimulating effects of estrogen and inhibitory effects of androgens on male breast tissue.

Stromal and ductal proliferation in gynecomastia progresses from an early florid stage characterized by intraductal epithelial hyperplasia and a loose, cellular stroma to a late quiescent fibrous stage characterized by hyalinized stroma.
A careful history, including a detailed review of medications and over-the-counter preparations, will help in establishing potential causes of gynecomastia. C
Physical examination establishes the diagnosis of gynecomastia by palpation of breast tissue in periareolar area. C
Examination of testis and if any abnormality suspected, appropriate evaluation. C
Biochemical evaluation may be useful in patients without an obvious etiology. Renal, liver fuction tests, and endocrine evaluation may be obtained. C
Mammography should not be used as a routine imaging procedure in men without clinically suspicious lesions. B
All lesions suspicious for malignancy should be biopsied regardless of mammographic findings. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Increased subareolar fat without enlargement of the breast glandular component
Tissue is hard or firm, located outside the nipple-areolar complex, most often unilateral

May be indistinguishable clinically and radiologically from gynecomastia; histologically characterized by connective tissue overgrowth with vasculitis and some proliferation of duct epithelium; benign condition, seen in patients with long-standing diabetes with other complications

list.listitem: A careful history, including a detailed review of medications and drugs with abuse potential, will help in establishing the potential causes of gynecomastia.

Drugs and drug classes associated with gynecomastia include antiandrogens for prostate cancer, estrogens, spironolactone, ketoconazole, calcium channel blockers, isoniazid, metronidazole, metoclopramide, and phenothiazines. Drugs of abuse associated with gynecomastia include alcohol, marijuana, and amphetamines.
In addition to examination of the breast, examine the testicles to assess the presence of atrophy (suggesting estrogenic effects) or masses.

To examine the breasts, place the patient supine with his hands behind his head. Using the thumb and forefinger, bring the fingers together from either side of the breast. An examiner would feel a rubbery or firm mound of tissue around nipple-areolar complex in a patient with true gynecomastia.
Gynecomastia is unilateral in approximately half the cases.

Some experts suggest biochemical evaluation in patients with acute onset of painful gynecomastia or in patients without an obvious cause to rule out potential serious causes or treatable etiologies. This testing includes the following: serum creatinine, liver function, thyroid-stimulating hormone, testosterone, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, prolactin, estradiol, DHEA sulfate, and serum beta-hCG.
Perform a karyotype in patients with suspected Klinefelter syndrome.

Mammography is accurate in patients with gynecomastia and in diagnosing breast cancer.However, since the frequency of cancer in men referred for evaluation of lumps is approximately 1%, mammography is unnecessary in most men and should not be used as a routine imaging procedure in all patients with gynecomastia.
Mammography is recommended if there is a clinical suspicion of malignancy. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy should be performed if breast cancer is suspected either clinically or radiographically.

Tamoxifen (10 mg twice daily) reduces breast size and decreases pain in men with idiopathic gynecomastia. B
In men with idiopathic gynecomastia, danazol (200 mg twice daily for 3 months) is more effective than placebo in decreasing the rate of surgery (NNT = 5) and in improving breast pain. B

Tamoxifen is the recommended medical therapy for men with gynecomastia associated with prostate cancer treatment, and also for the prevention of gynecomastia in men undergoing hormonal therapy for prostate cancer (NNT = 2). B
Most patients with gynecomastia do not require intervention.
Tamoxifen and danazol have been helpful in treating patients with gynecomastia from a variety of causes.

In a small randomized double-blind crossover study, 7 of 10 men taking tamoxifen (10 mg twice daily) had a reduction in breast size compared with 0 taking placebo. Additionally, of 4 men with painful gynecomastia, all had reductions in pain while taking tamoxifen. Finally, 9 months after the discontinuation of tamoxifen, most men had sustained benefits.

In a small double-blind RCT of men with idiopathic gynecomastia, 27% of men taking danazol (200 mg twice daily for 3 months) subsequently underwent surgery compared with 50% of men taking placebo (NNT = 5). In addition, the men taking danazol had improvements in breast pain.
Anastrozole was not found to be useful in achieving 50% reduction in breast size in boys between the ages of 11 and 18 years with pubertal gynecomastia.

In men with gynecomastia associated with prostate cancer treatment, tamoxifen was better than other therapies (flutamide, orchiectomy, etc.) in reducing breast pain. Tamoxifen also reduced breast size within 4 to 6 weeks.

Tamoxifen has been widely studied (in varying doses) for the prevention of gynecomastia in men undergoing hormonal therapy for prostate cancer. Approximately 10% of men receiving tamoxifen developed gynecomastia compared with approximately 70% of men receiving placebo or no therapy (NNT = ~2).
No clinical trials exist on the effectiveness of surgery in men with persistent gynecomastia.
In most circumstances, gynecomastia improves with time, weight loss, or by discontinuing medications associated with gynecomastia.
Most patients with gynecomastia do not require intervention; in pubertal boys, most gynecomastia resolves without intervention. C
The frequency of breast cancer in men referred for evaluation of gynecomastia is approximately 1%. B
